meta.subtitle: A wide-moat derivatives exchange with low, steady leverage, priced near fair value as second-quarter volumes cool

analystCommentary: CME Group runs the futures and options exchanges of CME, CBOT, NYMEX and COMEX and the clearing house behind them, and it turns that position into exceptional economics: a 64.9% operating margin in FY25, $83.5M of capital expenditure against $4.3B of operating cash flow, and $3.9B of dividends paid out of $4.2B of free cash flow. Leverage is low, at 0.3x net debt/EBITDA on a trailing basis. The second quarter is the reason for caution. Total revenue rose 1%, clearing and transaction fees fell 3% and the average rate per contract fell 2% as, in the company's account, market volatility subsided after a very volatile start to the year. At $276.01 the shares trade at 23.4x trailing earnings, with a split Street (7 Buy, 6 Hold, 3 Sell) and a $283.60 consensus target. We rate CME HOLD with a $250-$300 target range. Our Base follows the Street's median target on consensus earnings; the Bull adds an earnings beat at an unchanged multiple, and the Bear has earnings stall while the multiple falls. Weighted 20/55/25, the scenarios give a fair value of $277.25 and an expected upside of 0.4% against a bear-case downside of 16.7%. The franchise is not in question; the price already pays for it, and near-term earnings follow market volatility the company does not control.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: CME Group, founded in 1898 and headquartered in Chicago, operates contract markets for futures and options on interest rates, equity indexes, foreign exchange, energy, agricultural commodities and metals, and runs the clearing house that clears, settles and guarantees those contracts. It also runs cash markets in fixed income through BrokerTec and in foreign exchange through EBS. The company was known as Chicago Mercantile Exchange Holdings Inc. until July 2007. Revenue comes in three lines: clearing and transaction fees, which follow trading volume; market data and information services; and other. FY25 revenue was $6.5B at a 64.9% operating margin, with net income of $4.1B and diluted EPS of $11.16. The company reports a single segment and bills a substantial portion of its clearing and transaction fees to clearing firms. The business needs little capital and returns most of its cash to shareholders. The one input the model cannot set is trading volume, and the second quarter of 2026 is where that showed.

thesis.body: CME pairs a wide moat with a price that already reflects it, and the swing factor between the two is trading volume, which the company does not control. The liquidity in its benchmark contracts and the margin offsets of clearing them at one house keep customers in place, and the cost base is light enough that most revenue reaches shareholders. The second quarter showed the other side: volume and clearing fees slipped as volatility subsided, and consensus for FY26 needs a second-half pickup the quarter did not show. Our Base follows the Street's median and the weights lean slightly to the Bear, as the valuation section argues. The Bull needs the volatility of early 2026 to return; the Bear needs the second quarter's calm to last into 2027. Leverage is low and is not part of the debate. We hold because the weighted value sits close to the price.

catalysts: A return of the volatility behind the record first-quarter trading the company reported would lift volume, the line revenue is most geared to.
Market data keeps growing faster than the trading business, a stream that does not depend on volume; the growth section takes it up.
New products and venues are a further source of growth, which the growth section takes up.
Capital return continues through dividends and buybacks, as the cash-flow discussion sets out.
risks: Volume dependence: revenue follows market volatility, and the second quarter showed volume and clearing fees falling as volatility subsided.
Rate per contract: the average fee fell in the quarter for mix reasons the risk section sets out.
Valuation: with a consensus target 2.7% above the price, the shares carry little margin of safety.
Regulation: changes to tax or clearing-capital rules could raise costs for CME or its customers, as the risk section sets out.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue grew from $4.7B in FY21 to $6.5B in FY25, up 6.4% in the latest year, while operating income rose from $2.6B to $4.2B and diluted EPS from $7.29 to $11.16. The operating margin widened from 56.4% to 64.9% over the period because costs grew more slowly than revenue. An exchange has no cost of goods, so the gross-margin line is blank and operating margin carries the profitability read. The second quarter of 2026 is the cleaner read on the current run-rate. Total revenue of $1,706.2 million was up 1% year over year: clearing and transaction fees fell 3% to $1,352.5 million, market data and information services rose 20% to $238.1 million, and other revenue rose 9%. The average rate per contract fell to $0.678 from $0.690. Total expenses rose 6%, with technology at $83.3 million against $70.9 million and licensing and other fee agreements at $109.1 million against $96.2 million, so the quarter's operating margin fell from 66.7% a year earlier to the same level as the FY25 full-year margin. Below the operating line, non-operating income was $220.6 million, up 10%; it nets $1,429.7 million of investment income against $1,263.2 million of other non-operating expense and adds $97.7 million of equity in the earnings of unconsolidated subsidiaries. A lower effective tax rate, 21.5% against 22.9%, helped net income rise 2% to $1,041.8 million and diluted EPS to $2.88 from $2.81. The first half looks stronger because of the first quarter: six-month revenue rose 8%, diluted EPS rose 12% to $6.06 and the operating margin was 67.4%. The second quarter, with costs rising faster than revenue, is a reminder that the first half's pace leaned on an unusually volatile first quarter.
financials.balanceCommentary: CME's debt has been flat. Total debt was $3.4B in every year from FY21 to FY25, and long-term debt was $3,424.2 million at June 30, 2026. Against it, cash and short-term investments ran between $2.8B and $3.0B in FY21 to FY24, leaving net debt of $0.5B to $0.7B, before rising to $4.5B in FY25 and leaving net cash of about $1.0B at that year-end. Cash and cash equivalents then fell from $4,416.9 million at December 31, 2025 to $2,144.2 million at June 30, 2026, for the reasons the cash-flow discussion sets out. The earnings release puts cash at $2.3 billion, a broader figure that includes $200 million deposited with Fixed Income Clearing Corporation and held in other current assets; we use the release figure, which it sets against $3.4 billion of debt, so CME was again a net debtor at mid-year. On a trailing basis net debt/EBITDA reads 0.3x, a low but real figure. The pack leaves interest coverage blank; the income statement shows $43.6 million of interest and other borrowing costs in the second quarter against $1,107.1 million of operating income, so servicing the debt is not a constraint. The balance sheet also carries $158,110.7 million of performance bonds and guaranty fund contributions on both sides, which is why the current ratio sits near 1.0 (1.02 on a trailing basis); that collateral is posted by clearing members and is not CME's own capital. Shareholders' equity of $26,520.4 million at June 30, 2026 is smaller than the $17,175.3 million of trading-product intangibles and $10,505.8 million of goodwill combined, so book value says little about the economics. Leverage is low and stable, and the swing between net debt and net cash reflects how much cash the company holds before paying it out, not new borrowing. An earlier version of this report understated CME's debt; the figures here are corrected.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow rose from $2.4B in FY21 to $4.3B in FY25, and free cash flow tracked it, reaching $4.2B in FY25 at a 64.3% FCF margin, because capital expenditure was only $83.5M in FY25. Dividends paid rose every year, from $2.2B in FY21 to $3.9B in FY25, so the company paid out most of each year's free cash flow as dividends. The vendor table shows no share-repurchase line, while the earnings release reports $695 million of repurchases and about $468 million of dividends in the second quarter of 2026; we use the release. First-half 2026 operating cash flow was $2,207.0 million, up 1%. Distributions in the first half ran well ahead of earnings: shareholders' equity fell from $28,728.2 million at December 31, 2025 to the June 30 level the balance-sheet discussion gives despite $2,196.1 million of first-half net income, and that drawdown is what took the balance sheet from net cash back to net debt. The pack itemizes only the second quarter's dividends and buybacks. The policy is coherent for a business that needs little reinvestment: debt has stayed flat while the surplus goes out. The cost is a thinner cash cushion than at the FY25 year-end, which matters only if volume and cash generation fall together.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $276.01 CME trades at 23.4x trailing earnings, 14.7x sales and 22.2x EV/EBITDA on a trailing basis. EV/EBITDA sits close to the P/E for two reasons: net debt is small, so enterprise value is close to the market capitalization of about $99.2B, and net income is close to EBITDA, because the non-operating investment income itemized in the financials offsets depreciation and tax. Two forward multiples appear in the pack. The snapshot shows about 21.4x on FY27E EPS of $12.93; the multiples block shows 22.5x labelled NTM, which lines up with the FY26E estimate of $12.25, so we read it as a current-year multiple. When we value the shares a year out on next year's earnings, the like-for-like reference is that NTM multiple, and all three scenarios are measured against it. The dividend yield is 1.88% and the trailing FCF yield 4.2%. The Street is divided: 16 analysts split Buy 7, Hold 6 and Sell 3 for a consensus Hold, with a consensus target of $283.60, a median of $285.00 and a range of $230.00-$330.00. The price sits near the middle of a 52-week range of $218.31-$329.16, well below the high, and the width of that range shows how far the shares have moved within a year. No peer column exists in this pack, so the multiples are judged against CME's own earnings path rather than against other exchanges. On that path, the multiples are full but not stretched for a franchise growing earnings at the mid-single-digit pace FY27E consensus implies.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Volatility returns at something like the early-2026 level, when the company reported record first-quarter trading and first-half EPS rose 12%. Volume and market data run ahead of plan, and FY27 EPS lands close to a tenth above the consensus. We hold today's 22.5x current-year multiple rather than raise it, because a beat driven by volatility is cyclical and gives the market no reason to pay more per dollar of earnings. That gives $315, below both the top of the Street's target range, $330.00, and the 52-week high of $329.16.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Second-half volume runs between the first quarter's surge and the second quarter's calm, enough for EPS to reach consensus of $12.25 for FY26E and $12.93 for FY27E, with market data still growing. A year out the multiple on FY27E earnings slips slightly below today's current-year multiple, because growth slows to the mid-single digits. That gives $285.00, the Street's median target. Holding today's multiple would put the Base a little higher without changing the label.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The second quarter's calm lasts into 2027: volatility stays low, interest-rate and energy volume keep falling, and the rate per contract keeps slipping. FY26 EPS ends a little below the FY26E consensus and does not grow in FY27. With growth gone, the multiple on that EPS falls to the high teens, well below today's current-year multiple, as investors stop paying for growth. That gives $230.00, the bottom of the Street's target range, still above the 52-week low of $218.31.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: All three scenarios value the shares a year out as a P/E on next year's earnings, measured against today's current-year multiple: the Bull holds that multiple on EPS above consensus, the Base trims it slightly on consensus EPS, and the Bear cuts it to the high teens on flat EPS. Two of the three prices coincide with Street targets, the Base with the median and the Bear with the bottom of the range, so the weighted value largely re-weights the Street's own view and lands close to its consensus. We weight the Base at 55% because consensus already assumes slower growth for FY27E, and the second quarter, though softer than a year earlier, still produced average daily volume of 29.8 million contracts, which the company ranks third among its quarters. The Bear gets 25% against the Bull's 20% because the latest quarter sits closer to the Bear's premise than to the Bull's; the tilt is small because volatility is two-sided and the first quarter showed how quickly it can return. The scenarios give a weighted fair value of $277.25, an expected upside of 0.4% and a bear-case downside of 16.7%, for a reward/risk of 0.03x. That is a HOLD, and it is not close: swapping the Bull and Bear weights still derives HOLD, and SELL would need the Bear to carry about half the weight. The $250-$300 target range brackets the Base.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: CME reports a single segment, but its product complexes moved in different directions in the second quarter of 2026. Aggregate average daily volume fell 1% to 29,843 thousand contracts. Interest rates, at 14,532 thousand contracts a day, fell 6% and energy fell 13%, which the company tied to more certainty about Federal Reserve policy and to price stabilization in energy. Equity indexes rose by as much as energy fell and agricultural commodities also gained, while foreign exchange fell 10% and metals were flat. Electronic trading was 94% of volume. The single segment therefore hides real diversification: no one complex decides the result, though interest rates carry more volume than any other complex, and a soft quarter in rates and energy was partly cushioned by gains elsewhere.

moatFactors.name: Liquidity network effect
moatFactors.body: A futures market is useful only if it is liquid, and liquidity draws more of itself. The FY25 10-K, filed February 26, 2026, describes the reverse loop: a reduction in trading volume could make its markets less attractive as a source of liquidity, which could lead to a further loss of volume. The same loop protects the incumbent. A competitor must win liquidity before it can win trades, and CME's benchmark products across all major asset classes give it that position across the board.

moatFactors.name: Cross-margined clearing
moatFactors.body: CME clears what it trades, and clearing correlated positions at one house lets participants offset margin. The company says it provided more than $95 billion in daily margin efficiencies in the second quarter of 2026. A participant who moves one product elsewhere gives up part of that saving, which makes open interest sticky in a way a trading venue alone could not achieve.

moatFactors.name: Regulatory status
moatFactors.body: CME's exchanges and clearing house operate as designated contract markets and a derivatives clearing organization under a regime the 10-K describes as imposing significant costs and competitive burdens. That cost raises the bar for any new entrant, which would also need to draw liquidity away from established benchmarks. The same regulation can constrain CME, which the risk section takes up.

moatFactors.name: Capital-light economics
moatFactors.body: The model needs little capital, so most incremental revenue reaches cash. That lets CME fund technology and new products from a small share of cash flow and still pay most of it out, an advantage over any rival that must invest heavily to compete for the same liquidity.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat WIDE with high confidence. Liquidity and cross-margining reinforce each other, and the regulatory barrier sits on top of both. The limits on durability come from outside the competitive position: regulation, which the risk section takes up, and volume, which rises and falls with market volatility however strong the moat is. Longer term, the open questions are new venues and products and how the shift of infrastructure to Google Cloud performs. What the price assumes is not only that the moat holds, which we expect, but that volume keeps growing into it, and that part is cyclical.

points: Consensus sees FY26E revenue of about $7B (+8%) and EPS of $12.25, then FY27E revenue of $7.4B and EPS of $12.93, a slowdown to mid-single-digit growth in the second year. FY26E needs the second half to grow faster than the second quarter did, so the estimate leans on volume recovering rather than holding at second-quarter levels.
Market data is the steadiest growth line. It rose 18% in the first six months of 2026 even as trading volume softened in the second quarter, and the second-quarter gain was faster still.

Retail adoption of micro contracts is a source of volume: the company credits precious-metals micro contracts among its retail client base with sustaining metals volume growth after demand eased in gold. Those contracts carry a lower fee, as the risk section explains, so this growth adds less revenue than the volume suggests.

New products are optional upside not yet in the figures: Single-Stock futures, 1-Ounce Gold contracts available 24/7, U.S. Treasury clearing, Compute futures, and sports-index futures with FutureSports.

The move to Google Cloud is a cost question as much as a growth one: the July 22, 2026 earnings release flags variable costs and duplicative on-premise and cloud costs during the transition, and the technology expense growth noted in the financials is the place it would show.

management.leadership: The March 2026 proxy names Terrence A. Duffy as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer and Lynne C. Fitzpatrick as President and Chief Financial Officer, with titles as of December 31, 2025; the July 22, 2026 earnings release still identifies Terry Duffy as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. The other named executive officers were Derek L. Sammann, Global Head of Commodities Markets, Julie M. Winkler, Chief Commercial Officer, and Sunil K. Cutinho, Chief Information Officer. On execution, the core business is run well: margins stayed high through a soft volume quarter. The weaker sign is cost growth outpacing revenue in the second quarter, and the initiatives management promotes, from new contracts to the cloud migration, are not yet visible in revenue. We weight the base business, which is strong, above the initiatives, which are unproven.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is simple. The record shows flat debt, little spending on capital projects, and the rest paid out through dividends and buybacks, as the cash-flow discussion details. For a business with this cash conversion and low leverage, that is the right default. The first-half 2026 payout the cash-flow discussion describes leaves less cushion if a low-volatility stretch lasts, though it is not a strain at current leverage. Among the factors the company lists in its July 22, 2026 earnings release is its ability to continue to generate funds and manage its indebtedness; nothing in the pack suggests pressure there.
management.governance: The governance view rests on the DEF 14A filed March 23, 2026. The board requires a majority of independent directors and fully independent audit, compensation, and nominating and governance committees, under categorical standards the company says conform to and exceed Nasdaq's. At the 2025 annual meeting approximately 87% of shareholders voted for the advisory resolution on executive pay. 2025 bonuses reflected cash earnings at about 114.3% of the target goal, performance shares from the September 2022 award vested at 200.0% of target in March 2026, and the September 2025 grants tie half of the performance shares to total shareholder return relative to the S&P 500 and half to absolute net income margin over 2026-2028. Two features concentrate influence: the chairman and chief executive roles are combined, and members of CME, some of whom sit on the board, can elect six directors. The independent majority and independent committees are the counterweight, and the nominating and governance committee reviews member directors' trading for independence, so we see a structure holders should understand rather than a red flag. The pay outcomes look aligned with results: net income grew in FY25, as the financials show, and the net-income-margin metric rewards protecting the margin this thesis rests on.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt in the pack covers board independence, the member-director election right and the compensation framework, but it does not quantify director or officer share ownership, so we assert no insider-ownership figure.

idiosyncratic: Volume dependence is the main risk and is already visible. Revenue follows volume, and volume follows market volatility; the second-quarter declines came, in the company's account, as volatility subsided from an elevated first quarter. A long low-volatility stretch would press on the core revenue line while costs keep rising, which is the Bear case.

The average rate per contract fell in the second quarter and the first half. The company attributes the drop largely to more micro-contract volume in equities, energy and metals and a higher share of member trading, partly offset by fee increases that took effect on April 1, 2026. If those mix shifts continue, revenue can fall even when volume holds.

One clearing firm accounted for at least 10% of clearing and transaction fees in the first six months of 2026. The company believes the customer portion of a departing firm's activity would likely move to another clearing firm, which is a reasonable view for a market where the liquidity sits with the exchange, but a firm's own trading would not necessarily follow.

Regulation is a standing risk. The FY25 10-K flags possible transaction taxes, rules that could require more of the company's funds for the guaranty fund, and litigation over the legal status of event contracts, with that litigation's status as of the filing. Either of the first two would raise costs for CME or its customers and could reduce volume. Heavy regulation also protects the franchise, so the exposure cuts both ways.

Clearing carries a tail risk. CME guarantees cleared contracts, and among the factors listed in its July 22, 2026 earnings release are the ability of its credit and liquidity risk management to protect it from the credit risks of clearing firms and other counterparties, and to meet margin and liquidity needs in the BrokerTec matched principal business. The probability is low but the severity would be high.
risks.systemic: CME's link to the market cycle is unusual. The 10-K notes that periods of heightened uncertainty have tended to increase trading volume through hedging and speculation, so a shock that hurts most companies can help CME, as the first quarter of 2026 showed. The relationship is not simple: the same filing warns that after a material market disturbance, extreme uncertainty may persist and reduce volume, and a long calm is plainly bad for the business. Interest rates matter in two ways. Uncertainty about Federal Reserve policy drives the interest-rate complex, which the company said softened in the second quarter as that uncertainty eased, and the earnings release lists variances in earnings on the cash and collateral its clearing house holds among the factors that might affect results. Policy risk sits on top: beyond the tax and capital rules the risk list covers, the release also names a possible repeal of the 60/40 tax treatment of futures, and the cloud migration adds a dependence on third-party technology providers. Most of these exposures are stabilizing, and several cut both ways.

body: We rate CME Group HOLD with a $250-$300 target range. The scenarios give a weighted fair value of $277.25 against the $276.01 price, an expected upside of 0.4% and a bear-case downside of 16.7%. The franchise is of high quality: liquidity in benchmark contracts, cross-margined clearing and a regulated position support a wide moat, the operating margin is near 65% and capital needs are small. Leverage stays low, as the balance-sheet discussion sets out.

The HOLD comes from the price against the moment. The valuation already pays for the quality, the Street is split, and the second quarter showed volume, clearing fees and the rate per contract all softening as volatility eased, while consensus for FY26 still needs a second-half pickup. As the valuation section sets out, the Base tracks the Street's median target and the weighting tilts a little toward the Bear.

On the same scenarios, the page's math would derive BUY a little above the low end of our range and SELL a little below its top. Beyond price, we would turn more positive if volume and the rate per contract recover together and EPS runs ahead of the FY26E consensus. We would turn more cautious if third-quarter results extend the second quarter's declines, the rate per contract keeps falling despite the April fee increases, or a transaction tax or higher guaranty-fund requirement advances.
